response.consequence: A deployment that has both the FIPS and the default or Elytron crypto jars on its classpath used to fail fast. It can now start with the non-FIPS provider, depending on jar order, and nobody is told. That silently breaks FIPS compliance and makes crypto behaviour nondeterministic between environments.
response.explanation: The change removes the "multiple crypto providers" failure in detectProvider. It replaces it with a sort by order() and takes the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200 from order(). When two of them are on the classpath, the sort ties. The sort is stable, so the winner is whichever ServiceLoader lists first, which depends on classpath or jar order. The only trace of the ignored providers is a debug-level log line.
response.title: Tied crypto provider order silently picks an arbitrary provider (including non-FIPS over FIPS)

response.consequence: A FIPS deployment that also has the non-FIPS default provider on the classpath can silently run non-FIPS crypto, or the chosen provider can change with jar ordering. This is a compliance and security risk. Third-party CryptoProvider implementations also break at compile time until they add order().
response.explanation: detectProvider used to throw when more than one CryptoProvider was found. It now sorts by order() descending and takes the first. DefaultCryptoProvider returns 200, WildFlyElytronProvider returns 200 and FIPS1402Provider returns 200. Only AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100. The sort is stable, so for providers with equal order the winner is whichever ServiceLoader lists first, and that follows classpath order. If a FIPS jar and the default jar are both on the classpath, either can be selected. The former check that failed on this misconfiguration is gone, and it is now only a debug log of the ignored providers. The new interface method order() is abstract, so any third-party CryptoProvider fails to compile until it implements it. I did not check whether any server artifact bundles both the default and FIPS provider jars, or whether the authz-client jar can end up on the server classpath. If it does, it loses with 100 against 200, so that case is handled.
response.title: Tied order() values make crypto provider selection depend on classpath order

response.explanation: The new test file only calls methods that exist in AuthzClientCryptoProvider (getEcdsaCryptoProvider, asn1derToConcatenatedRS, concatenatedRSToASN1DER) with signatures that match. The round trip DER to R||S to DER to R||S is sound for ES256, ES384 and ES512, including when a P-256 key signs with a longer hash, because the R and S values are padded to the target length.
response.title: No API compatibility defect in the new ECDSA round-trip test

response.consequence: Malformed or non-canonical ECDSA signatures can be accepted. Short input produces an unexpected runtime exception. The impact is limited because this is a minimal client-side provider.
response.explanation: In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes drops the high-order bytes when the BigInteger's byte array is longer than qLength. A DER signature whose r or s is larger than the curve order size is not rejected. Its low len bytes are used instead, so the check passes on a different value. A DER signature with extra high bytes therefore verifies as if it were the canonical one, which makes the signature malleable. Negative DER integers are also accepted, because their two's-complement bytes are copied. concatenatedRSToASN1DER also does not check that signature.length is at least signLength. A short input throws an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from System.arraycopy instead of an IOException. Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder results and discard them. The ES512 sizes are correct: signLength is 132, len is 66, and the len+1 buffer with a leading zero gives non-negative values.
response.title: integerToBytes silently truncates oversized r/s; redundant encoder calls

response.consequence: No concrete failing input attributable to this change was identified.
response.explanation: The change only adds CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) and test-scoped junit/hamcrest dependencies. AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered through the META-INF service file and is designed as a minimal provider. It supports the ECDSA conversion and returns the default KeyStore provider. Its other methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. I found no evidence that the authz-client paths previously worked through a fuller crypto provider. Without this init call, crypto provider lookups would not have a provider at all. The unsupported methods are therefore not a regression introduced by this change.
response.title: No regression shown from CryptoIntegration.init in AuthzClient.create

response.consequence: A malformed signature can raise an unchecked exception that callers do not handle, instead of the IOException the API declares. The effect is limited to a failed or crashed signature conversion.
response.explanation: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length byte 0x80. readInteger() passes that value straight to read(length), which runs new byte[-1] and throws NegativeArraySizeException. A zero-length INTEGER makes new BigInteger(new byte[0]) throw NumberFormatException. asn1derToConcatenatedRS declares only IOException, so callers cannot expect these. The input is an untrusted DER signature, for example 30 06 02 80 ... or 30 02 02 00.
response.title: ASN1Decoder.readInteger throws unchecked exceptions on malformed DER lengths

response.consequence: A crafted ECDSA signature with an empty INTEGER makes verification fail with an unchecked exception instead of the expected IOException or a clean invalid-signature result. This can bypass callers' error handling.
response.explanation: readInteger passes the content bytes to new BigInteger(bytes) with no check that length > 0. A signature such as 30 04 02 00 02 00 passes readSequence (two elements, each [02 00]). readInteger then reads length 0 and calls new BigInteger(new byte[0]), which throws NumberFormatException ("Zero length BigInteger"). It does not throw IOException. The caller asn1derToConcatenatedRS declares only IOException and does not catch runtime exceptions. Other malformed input, such as truncated or oversized lengths, does produce IOException. The tag and length arithmetic in readNext (mark, count, reset) is correct for 1-byte and 2-byte lengths and for a leading 0x00 in r or s. Indefinite lengths cannot reach new byte[-1], because readNext returns only the tag byte for them and readInteger then hits EOF.
